text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Sweden wants to be able to increase its discharge of carbon dioxide by at least five percent by the year 2010 according to its negotiations with the European Union. Most EU countries are having difficulties agreeing on rules of climate regulation but Sweden is set to agree on a five percent lift.

- Swedish egg producers have come under criticism for poor control of laying hens, giving rise to the threat of salmonella. The lack of adequate testing procedures has come to light as European Union inspectors could at any time come to Sweden to examine the industry and Swedish food exports.

- The government is set to change the management of state-controlled power company Vattenfall after the newly agreed energy package, according to a newspaper source. Vattenfall is to take a more active role in the energy system.

- Swedish vehicle manufacturer Volvo will spend more on international subcontractors when it starts production of the new 90 model next year. Chairman of the company's components unit, Lars Holmqvist, said among the eight or nine subcontractors to be used there was no Swedish group.

- Swedish nuclear power plant Barseback, located at the southern tip of Sweden close to Denmark, has insufficient safety routines, according to the nuclear power inspectorate. The authority pointed to insufficient routines two years ago and they have not yet fully improved. The inspectorate could keep the plant under surveillance until the closure of one reactor in 1998. The government and two other parties this week agreed to shut down one of the plant's two reactors in 1998 and the other in 2001. The plant is owned by Swedish power company Sydkraft which has asked for compensation for the closure.

- The crown has weakened so much that it could make the central bank, the Riksbank, refrain from cutting its key repurchase rate any further, according to share, currency and securities dealers. The Riksbank attempted to halt the crown's softening on Wednesday by buying the currency following a crown weakening of around six percent in three months. The Riksbank has not cut the repo rate this year. In 1996 it cut it to the current level of 4.10 percent from 8.91 percent.

- Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson promised on Wednesday to spend six billion crowns, mainly on municipalities and regional authorities, to keep unemployment from surging. The money will come from a reallocation of different ministries' funds and is intended to keep local and regional authorities from laying off more people.

- Head of airline SAS, Jan Stenberg and two of his associates will travel to Toulouse in France to meet the management of Airbus Industrie. The SAS trio will talk to Airbus about its plans to replace the Scandinavian airline's fleet of 14 Boeing 767 planes, a deal worth over 10 billion crowns.

- President of Swedish media group Mareiberg, Carl-Johan Bonnier, has dismissed criticism from the Minister of Culture Marita Ulvskog about his group's acquisition of a large slice of the country's largest commerical television station, TV4. He said the minister's comments that this buy will lead to too much power in the hands of the Bonnier family were absurd and old fashioned. He said there was no proof that a concentration of control over the media in itself was bad.

- Sweden's plan to dismantle nuclear power and Prime Minister Goran Persson's recent pledge to give county governments an extra 10 billion crowns a year has made money traders abroad nervous. London-based analysts of Swedish securities say the credibility of the Swedish government has been damaged. The spread between Swedish and German 10-year bonds was about 75 basis points a month ago but has now widened to 120 basis points.
